historical_record.description: Following the Chamber of Commerce's Civic Development Committee, the Recreation and Park Commission reported to the Board of Supervisors that the Palace of Fine Arts should not be restored.

The Recreation and Park Commission asked the Board of Supervisors to put the demolition or restoration of the Palace of Fine Arts to the voters, and said that otherwise it would budget for demolishing the Palace and restoring the site as a public park.

Thanking Walter S. Johnson for his $2,000,000 gift toward rehabilitating the Palace of Fine Arts, the Recreation and Park Commission resolved that the most important part of the restored Palace be named and dedicated in his honor, the part to be chosen once the plans were final.

The Director of Public Works told the Recreation and Park Commission that the low bid for restoring the Palace of Fine Arts under the Cahill Plan, from Frank Modglin, was $6,600,000, $1,600,000 more than the money available; the Commission let the Mayor's study committee explore the alternatives, among them John Cahill's suggestion to leave out the urns and part of the colonnades for later.

The Recreation and Park Commission approved an agreement with Vincent G. Raney, architect, for preliminary plans of a little theater of about 1,000 seats in the Palace of Fine Arts, estimated at $562,000, on condition that no further fee be paid if the plans were not approved or money for building it was not found.

The Recreation and Park Commission approved Vincent Raney's final plans and specifications for the little theater inside the Palace of Fine Arts, adding an alternate to rebuild or repair the part of the Palace roof over it. In February it had approved his preliminary plans, subject to the state parks division, and accepted Walter S. Johnson's gift of $250,000 toward the theater.

The Recreation and Park Commission approved Vincent G. Raney's plans for improvements to the Palace of Fine Arts building, among them a theater entrance, an enlarged lobby and a marquee, to be given by the Palace of Fine Arts League through Walter S. Johnson.

The Recreation and Park Commission accepted Walter S. Johnson's offer, through the Palace of Fine Arts League, to restore the Palace's north and south colonnades, and approved the plans by Hans Gerson, architect of the original rehabilitation; Gerson said the colonnades had been an approved alternate in 1963 but were left out of the contract for want of money.

Hans U. Gerson, for the Palace of Fine Arts League, showed the Recreation and Park Commission his plans, already passed by the Art Commission, to enlarge the Palace of Fine Arts theater lobby, separating the concession area from the foyer and adding a proper box office, paid for by a $90,000 gift from Walter Johnson.

The rebuilt colonnades of the Palace of Fine Arts, given by Walter S. Johnson through the Palace of Fine Arts League at a cost of $1.4 million, were dedicated on Sunday, October 5, as the general manager reported to the Recreation and Park Commission.
The Recreation and Park Commission awarded Gomez-Chapot a $597,600 contract for the seismic upgrade of the Palace of Fine Arts.

Following the seismic contract, the Recreation and Park Commission approved disability access work at the Palace of Fine Arts: parking, paths of travel, access within the building and accessible restrooms.

With the Stephenson Construction Company the low bidder at $38,600 to rebuild the structural portion of the Palace of Fine Arts' colonnades and rotunda, the Board of Park Commissioners asked the Board of Public Works to let and supervise the contract, none of it to be paid from park funds.
